source.title: Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration
source.authors: Aashiq Muhamed; Mona T. Diab; Virginia Smith

page_placements.theme: Robustness to direction-based removal: training against ablation, decoys, hidden switches, and removal routes that bypass the direction

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates DIM-based refusal ablation and automated weight-level removal attacks, but its main intervention is a post-hoc defense rather than a direct reproduction of the original single-direction intervention. It also tests whether higher-rank and iterative attacks overcome rank-1 protection.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own outcomes for standard RFA, Heretic, ReFAT under RFA, adaptive multi-phase RFA, and rank-k RFA. DDO’s probe counts and optimization hyperparameters are setup choices, not outcome rows. Prompt-level jailbreak results are not rows for V3 because the paper does not measure whether those attacks suppress the claimed direction; the proposed GCG mechanism is explicitly a plausible explanation. Cited findings from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly a defense (DDO), but it reports its own refusal-removal results on undefended models. Per-layer DIM ablation gives 66.5–90.7% ASR on six instruct models, which bears on V1. Heretic weight-level abliteration gives 88.7% on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, which bears on V2. ReFAT checkpoints, trained against DIM ablation, are tested under RFA, Heretic, adaptive RFA and GCG, which bears on V3. The ablation differs from the original: all 32 per-layer directions are ablated at once rather than one selected direction. DDO-defended results measure the study's own defense corrupting the estimator, not refusal geometry, so they fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude DDO, a cheap post-hoc weight edit that corrupts the attacker's DIM estimator, matches trained defenses on standard RFA across six families (<10% ASR) at 30–450× lower cost. They add that it degrades under sustained adaptive re-estimation (65% vs 58% worst case) and higher-rank attacks. Under Heretic it reaches 18% versus RepBend's 1.3%. They frame it as a cost-raising layer, not a guarantee.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-safe DIM and projection-based RFA, but estimates and ablates per-layer directions simultaneously at specified hookpoints rather than selecting a single layer-position direction as in the original pipeline. The main intervention is DDO, a post-hoc MLP weight edit.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack rank and adaptive phase change ASR; decoy-reader count K changes the rank-1 versus higher-rank tradeoff. DDO also depends on model-specific layer placement and compile mode, as reported in the paper.

fits_no_version.finding: A post-hoc nonlinear decoy edit (DDO) makes standard DIM ablation fail (0–8% ASR) while refusal persists. Rank-k SVD attacks (79% at k=32) and adaptive re-estimation (65% worst case) recover much of it. Linear defenses (rotation, shear) are defeated once DIM is re-estimated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The contrastive DIM estimate of the refusal direction can be adversarially corrupted by weight edits; higher-rank or iterative re-estimation largely restores abliteration.

record.problems: The standard-RFA protocol differs from the original direction-selection procedure: the authors apply per-layer directions simultaneously and call this a larger ablation budget. Most ASR results do not report error bars, although the paper notes seed variation for DIM and Heretic. The reported capability metrics generally describe defended checkpoints, not utility after standard RFA ablation. ReFAT is a comparator rather than an isolated causal test of training against ablation.
record.rows_left_out: None. The paper's prompt-level jailbreak ASR results are not included because they do not measure whether those attacks suppress the direction; the paper only offers that as a plausible explanation for GCG. Additional DDO utility metrics are not rows for V1 because utility was not measured after the RFA ablation itself.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal. Single selected-direction ablation; the paper ablates all 32 per-layer directions at once. Capability after standard RFA is reported only as MT-Bench after adaptive phase 1 on base Llama-3.
Capability after the Heretic edit, beyond a KL flag. Released models other than Llama-3-8B-Instruct.
Whether prompt jailbreaks suppress the direction; the GCG link is offered only as a plausible explanation.
Not tested: rank-k and adaptive results exist only on DDO-defended models.
Not tested; directions are estimated per model.

missing.what: Undefended Llama-3 under adaptive RFA: 73% ASR at phase 1 with MT-Bench 7.89→7.47. Bears on V1's 'other abilities largely kept'.
Undefended Llama-3 three-point RFA ASR of 80% (LlamaGuard-2, JailbreakBench) as a single-judge reference.
Undefended per-layer single-layer ablation causal zones and baseline refusal rates across 7 models (e.g., Qwen3 base refusal 37%).
ReFAT Llama-3 Heretic ASR 85.3% and LAT 82.3%, against base 88.7%.
ReFAT adaptive RFA trajectory (worst case 60%) with MT-Bench collapsing to 2.46 at phase 1.
ReFAT prompt-jailbreak ASR: GCG 30.6, PAIR 30.0, HJB 0.0, AutoDAN 0.0, against base 27.7/55.1/2.9/0.4.
ReFAT utility costs: Llama-3 XSTest 60.4%; GLM-4 MT-Bench 2.84; Yi MT-Bench 6.60.

record.verdict_notes: Undefended rows use all-32-layer simultaneous DIM ablation with unfiltered probes, a larger budget than the original's single-direction selection. Several base models (Yi, Mistral, GLM) already comply 26–41% without ablation. The record's V1 limits_scope from DDO rows and its V4 labels were removed: those rows test the study's own defense, not natural refusal geometry. ReFAT cross-model checkpoints are the authors' reproductions; the Llama-3 one is a public checkpoint.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests DIM-based ablation and reports harmful compliance, but does not test whether adding the direction induces refusal on harmless requests. Its capability scores are not measured after the RFA ablation itself.
Tests Heretic on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, including with DDO; weight-edit removal is not reported for all released models.

Tests robustness from ReFAT training against RFA, but does not directly measure whether prompt-level jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction. The GCG explanation is presented as plausible, not established.
Tests higher-rank and iterative ablation outcomes, but does not directly compare affine or cone descriptions of refusal geometry.
No direct test separating harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
Per-model DDO and per-model DIM evaluations are not tests of transfer of one direction across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No experiment varies when or how refusal training is performed to determine whether a removable direction exists.

relation.reason: It reports attack results on undefended and ReFAT models, not only its own defense's performance.

tranche.reason: Its own results bear on V1, V2 and V3: undefended RFA, Heretic, and ReFAT comparators. The method differs from the original: per-layer last-token DIM at all layers without KL selection, scored by 3-judge ASR.

source_check.notes: ASR is a 3-judge harmfulness average, not a refusal rate. Utility columns describe checkpoints before attack. Base Llama-3 adaptive Phase 1 gives 73% ASR with only a 0.3-point MT-Bench drop, which bears on V1 capability but is in no row. Table 9 single-layer causal zones (Llama-3: 8/32 layers) are not recorded either.

statements.problem: Numbers and conditions match Tables 2-3. 'DDO's standard RFA' means the paper's attack on undefended models, not RFA after DDO.
None for this study: Gemma-2-9B RFA 66.5%, DR 1.3%, other five 84.9-90.7% (Table 3).
None: 85.1% mean RFA with DR 3.8% (Table 2), per-layer last-token directions at all 32 layers (F.1).
None for this study. Its measure is the 3-judge avg ASR on JailbreakBench and HarmBench.

statements.correction: H-200 is the max-ASR trial of 200 Optuna trials, ±3% across 3 runs. Utility columns describe checkpoints before attack. Post-Heretic quality is only flagged by KL>0.3 daggers; base 88.7% is not daggered (F.1, F.13).
statements.problem: The 88.7% and 3.8% are right, but 'capability check' does not apply to the Heretic result: post-attack utility is not measured.

statements.correction: Llama-3 ReFAT is a publicly released checkpoint. Cross-model ReFAT models are LoRA reproductions, best of A/B/C configs (p_rfa 0.5/0.7/0.9) by lowest 3-judge RFA ASR (F.8). Prompts are JailbreakBench+HarmBench. Judges: HarmBench classifier, LlamaGuard-2, StrongREJECT. ReFAT Llama-3 XSTest is 60.4 vs base 94.8; the authors say this is partly over-refusal.
statements.problem: 'Re-evaluated ReFAT checkpoints' holds only for Llama-3. The Yi, Qwen3 and Gemma-2 ReFAT models are the authors' own reproductions. Prompt and judge details of this study are not given.

statements.correction: Heretic H-200: ReFAT 85.3% vs base 88.7% (Table 2). Adaptive RFA (LlamaGuard-2 only, Table 16): ReFAT phases 1-6 at 1-9%, then 60 (Ph7) and 46 (Ph8); worst 60 vs base worst 73. ReFAT MT-Bench is 2.46 at Phase 1 and 4.01 at Phase 8.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the adaptive 60% is a partial gain over the undefended model, not an absent effect. Only the Heretic result fits 'challenges'.
None: Mistral 86.3 to 57.6, GLM-4 87.0 to 52.9 (Table 3). GLM-4 ReFAT MT-Bench is also 2.84.

statements.correction: F.1: per-layer procedure is 'at least as strong as the single-direction variant under matched probe sets'. Llama-3 baselines use publicly released defended checkpoints (Sec 4.1, F.8); the source is not named. Heretic 85.3% and adaptive worst 60% (LlamaGuard-2) are right.
statements.problem: The text calls per-layer RFA 'at least as strong' as single-direction selection, not stronger. It does state where its Llama-3 ReFAT checkpoint came from.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Undefended instruction-tuned models under the paper's standard RFA protocol
reader_labels.reason: The reported RFA ASRs are high on the six undefended model rows, consistent with harmful compliance after DIM ablation (r1, r4, r6, r8, r10, r12).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: After DDO, standard-RFA ASR is 0.0–8.0% across the reported models, so the attack does not generally cause harmful compliance in these defended checkpoints (r2, r3, r5, r7, r9, r11, r13).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Heretic reaches 88.7% ASR on the undefended model, showing substantial refusal removal by a weight-level attack (r14).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: DDO lowers H-200 ASR from 88.7% to 18%, but the attack still has nonzero success (r15).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Yi-1.5-9B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2-9B under standard RFA
reader_labels.reason: The ReFAT-trained checkpoints have much lower standard-RFA ASR than their undefended references (r16–r19).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Mistral-7B and GLM-4-9B under standard RFA after ReFAT training
reader_labels.reason: ReFAT reduces ASR relative to base, but reported values remain 57.6% and 52.9% (r20, r21).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: DDO under adaptive multi-phase and higher-rank RFA on Llama-3-8B-Instruct
reader_labels.reason: Fresh re-estimation and higher-rank attacks raise harmful-compliance ASR; the rank-32 result reaches 79%, near the undefended 80% reference, and adaptive phases reach up to the paper's stated 65% worst case (r25–r29, r34, r35).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Lower-rank attacks and diversified-reader DDO settings
reader_labels.reason: Several tested lower-rank conditions retain low ASR, and the effect depends on attack rank and decoy-reader count; for example, the K=4 rank-1 value is 27% while its rank-2 and rank-4 values are 0% (r30–r33, r36–r55).
